summary: Vancouver's Brockton Point light in Stanley Park: a mast light from 1890, a wooden house in 1902, a concrete tower in 1914 or 1915, dark since 2008.

structures.note: Rowlett gives 1915; designer named by Rowlett as William P. Anderson, by the Vancouver Heritage Foundation as Colonel William Anderson

structures.name: wooden lighthouse with dwelling
structures.note: Building 29 ft (8.8 m) high; painted brown and yellow with red roof; light in a wooden lantern on the first floor
Red and white lanterns on a mast

access.note: In Stanley Park; the Stanley Park seawall passes under the tower's arched base

facts.agency: Vancouver Parks and Recreation Board (managed since 2006)

events.note: A mast with red and white lanterns at the point (the first light)
Day marks erected on Brockton Point to clear Parthia shoal; removed once the new lighthouse interrupted the range
Wooden lighthouse with dwelling attached, 85 feet (26 m) from the place where the light had been shown; reported in the 1902 report
Pole light replaced by the wooden lighthouse
Jones and a yacht's crew pulled a man from the harbour; Lighthouse Friends says he died of shock
Princess Victoria collided with the Chehalis near Brockton Point on 21 July 1906; the Chehalis sank
Steamer Charmer ashore in dense fog in Vancouver narrows near Brockton Point, 3 to 5 December 1908
Present tower; the Vancouver Heritage Foundation and a blog give 1914, Rowlett gives 1915
Semaphore at Brockton Point discontinued (Lighthouse Friends)
Management passed to the Vancouver Parks and Recreation Board
Light inactive; a decorative light may be displayed

corrections.why: 1890 is when the first light (a mast with red and white lanterns) went up. The present tower dates from 1914 (Vancouver Heritage Foundation and a blog) or 1915 (Rowlett).

resolved_conflicts.explanation: Wikidata's 1915 and the record's 1890 both describe real events. 1890 is the first light, a mast with lanterns. The present tower is 1914 (Vancouver Heritage Foundation, blog) or 1915 (Rowlett).

notes_for_editor: 1) The 1902 Marine report's keeper list (scan p.247) reads 'Janes, William D' in OCR; matched by position and by the 1907 list to William D. Jones; check the page image. 2) The 1902 Marine report (scan p.98) prints the printed page as uncertain (85?); cite is by scan page. 3) Tower date conflict: 1914 (Vancouver Heritage Foundation, blog) against 1915 (Rowlett, record). The 1916 and 1917 Marine reports (fiscal 1914-15 and 1915-16) have works lines naming 'Brockton point' and 'Erection of concrete tower and improvements to protection work between Brockton point and Prospect point'; the OCR columns do not tie those lines to a station by text alone, so they are not used in the story. Check the page image of 1917v52i13p21_1280 scan p.62 before relying on any year. 4) The Morning Call figure is OCR'd as '3% fathoms'; the story says only 'a few fathoms'. 5) Death toll: nine (Marine report 1907, Daily Alaskan, SF Call headline) against eight (Lighthouse Friends, blog); both given. 6) Direction of the Princess Victoria: Marine report and Western News (leaving Vancouver) against Daily Alaskan (coming in from Seattle); both given. 7) Lighthouse Friends is a community site: its facts (1905 rescue, semaphore 1909-1918, driftwood cottage, Duke's visit, focal plane) are attributed to it in the story and not checked against newspapers or reports. 8) Keepers after 1924 (Beck, Walsh, McLeod, Kilgour) are from the Vancouver Heritage Foundation only; the Marine corpus ends in 1924. 9) The Marine corpus starts in 1900 (no 1890s Canadian reports), so the first light and the 1890 start rest on secondary sources. 10) Charmer's dates: the casualty list is for fiscal 1908-09; the December 3 to 5 date is read as December 1908. 11) Not searched: British Columbia newspapers, which Chronicling America does not hold for 1890-1900; a BC newspaper search could confirm the 1890 light and Jones's 1905 rescue. 12) Checked on the page images in the fact-check: the 1908 statement of lightkeepers (scan p.199, printed p.190) gives W. D. Jones at Brockton Point, appointed 20 Aug 1890; that row is now cited as cite 17. The 1907 list (scan p.156) is not re-imaged; it agrees with the 1906, 1908 and 1911 lists. 13) The Chehalis is a steamer in the Marine report (cite 6) and a tug in the Western News (cite 10) and Lighthouse Friends (cite 13); the story gives both. 14) The Daily Alaskan 'arrest' item is a dispatch dated 23 July printed in the same issue as cite 8, not a later issue; the story no longer says 'two days later'. 15) Rowlett (cite 14) gives the owner as the Canadian Coast Guard and the site manager as the Vancouver Board of Parks and Recreation; the story says so. 16) The Morning Call figure (cite 4) is OCR'd as '3% fathoms'; the story says 'a few fathoms' and does not print the figure.
